threads.title: Hatred will not hear the commandment concerning loving one's neighbour
threads.summary_md: Gad warns that hatred worketh lawlessness even against the Lord, for it will not hear His commandments concerning the loving of one's neighbour. He names the precise Torah word it refuses — the command to love thy neighbour as thyself. It ain't new — the lawlessness of hatred is measured against the very statute Moses gave.

threads.title: Hatred worketh unto death, love unto salvation
threads.summary_md: Gad sets the two spirits side by side: the spirit of hatred worketh together with Satan unto men's death, but the spirit of love worketh together with the law of God in long-suffering unto the salvation of men. The apostle John draws the same line — we have passed from death unto life because we love the brethren. It ain't new — Gad's two spirits are John's two states, death and life, told beforehand.

threads.title: Humility destroyeth envy — and Gad's own liver judged
threads.summary_md: Gad teaches that humility destroyeth envy, and confesses that because his liver was set mercilessly against Joseph, in his liver too he suffered mercilessly — by what things a man transgresseth, by the same is he punished. Solomon names envy as the very rottenness of the bones. It ain't new — Gad's body bore in itself the proverb Israel already knew.

threads.title: Drive forth hatred which is of the devil — cleave to the love of God
threads.summary_md: Gad describes hatred mating with lying, kindling wrath and stirring up war, and bids his children drive it forth and cleave to the love of God. The apostle Paul gives the same charge — put away all bitterness, wrath, anger, and evil speaking. It ain't new — Gad's plea to cast out hatred is Paul's word to the saints, spoken long before.

threads.title: Love one another from the heart — put away hatred
threads.summary_md: The heart of Gad's testament: love one another from the heart, and put away hatred from your hearts — in deed, in word, and in the inclination of the soul. He had spoken peaceably to Joseph before his father while the spirit of hatred darkened his mind; now he commands the love Torah commands. It ain't new — love thy neighbour as thyself is Moses' own word, and the message John says was heard from the beginning.

threads.title: If a man sin against thee — rebuke, and if he repent, forgive him
threads.summary_md: Gad lays down the rule: if a man sin against thee, speak peaceably to him and hold no guile; if he repent and confess, forgive him. The Messiah gives word for word the same order — go and tell him his fault, and forgive thy brother seventy times seven. It ain't new — the Lord's forgiveness teaching and Gad's deathbed counsel are one path of rebuke-and-pardon.

threads.title: Even the shameless — forgive him from the heart, and leave to God the avenging
threads.summary_md: Gad reaches the hardest word: even if a man be shameless and persist in his wrong-doing, even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to God the avenging. Paul says forgive even as God forgave you; the Lord says forgive from your hearts; and vengeance belongs to God alone. It ain't new — heart-forgiveness that leaves vengeance to God is Moses, the Messiah, and the apostle in one voice.

threads.title: If a man prosper more than you, be not vexed but pray for him
threads.summary_md: Gad turns from hatred to its twin, envy: if a man prospereth more than you, be not vexed but pray for him; if he be exalted, be not envious. David's psalm gives the same medicine — fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be envious against the workers of iniquity. It ain't new — Gad's cure for envy is the song Israel already sang.

threads.title: Though a man grow rich by evil means as Esau — wait for the end of the Lord
threads.summary_md: Gad counsels that though a man become rich by evil means, even as Esau, be not jealous but wait for the end of the Lord — for the unrepentant is reserved for eternal punishment, while the poor man free from envy is blessed beyond all men. The psalm shows the same end: the wicked spreading like a green bay tree, yet passing away and found no more. It ain't new — the testament's patience is the psalmist's confidence in how the wicked end.

threads.title: Honour Judah and Levi — from them the Lord shall raise up salvation
threads.summary_md: Gad's closing charge before he falls asleep: tell your children to honour Judah and Levi, for from them shall the Lord raise up salvation to Israel. This is the testaments' joined hope — the sceptre of Judah and the priesthood of Levi meeting in one Anointed. It ain't new — Balaam saw the Star out of Jacob, and Zechariah saw the Branch who is priest upon his throne, the counsel of peace between the two.

threads.title: Asher's two ways — good and evil set before the sons of men
threads.summary_md: Asher opens his deathbed testament with the doctrine of the two ways: two ways God has given to the sons of men, two inclinations in the breast, the way of good and the way of evil, and the soul must cleave to one. This is the oldest framework in Scripture — Moses sets life and good over against death and evil and bids Israel choose; the Messiah narrows it to the strait gate and the broad way. It ain't new — the two ways the patriarch teaches are the two ways Deuteronomy and the Gospel set before every man.

threads.title: The two inclinations — repentance, or rule by Beliar
threads.summary_md: Asher describes the two inclinations warring in the breast: the soul that takes pleasure in the good repents straightway when it sins and uproots the evil, but the soul that inclines to the evil is ruled by Beliar, who perverts even its good to evil. The prophets and apostles know this same contest — sin conceived bringing forth death, and the heart drawn away by its own lust. It ain't new — the two inclinations Asher names are the lust that wars within and the new heart that turns and repents.

threads.title: The hare — half clean yet unclean, by the tables of the commandments
threads.summary_md: Asher's catalogue of the two-faced man ends in a striking figure: the man who sins greatly yet keeps some commandments, who fasts yet does evil, is like the hare — half clean, but in very deed unclean — for, he says, God in the tables of the commandments hath thus declared. The patriarch reaches straight for Torah's law of clean and unclean, where the hare is named unclean because it answers one mark of cleanness but not the other. It ain't new — Asher reads the two-faced soul off the very dietary law Moses wrote, and treats those commandments as standing and binding.

threads.title: He defraudeth his neighbour, yet pitieth the poor — the whole is evil
threads.summary_md: Among the two-faced men Asher exposes is the one who defrauds his neighbour, swears falsely, sets the law of the Lord at nought — and yet pities the poor, as though the one good covers the many evils. Torah forbids the very fraud and false swearing he indulges, and the Lord who commands the law is the One he provokes. It ain't new — Asher measures the double-faced almsgiver by the law of the Lord that he sets at nought.

threads.title: Wear not two faces — the double-minded who serve not God
threads.summary_md: Here is Asher's keystone charge: wear not two faces of goodness and of wickedness, but cleave to goodness only, for the double-faced serve not God but their own lusts, to please Beliar. This is the same single-heartedness the Messiah demands — no man can serve two masters — and the double-minded man James says is unstable in all his ways and must purify his heart. It ain't new — the two-faced man Asher warns against is the double-minded man Scripture calls to one Master and one heart.

threads.title: Men of single face — just before God, like the clean stag and hind
threads.summary_md: Asher turns to the good men of single face: though the double-faced think they sin, they are just before God; they are like stags and hinds, which seem wild and unclean but are altogether clean, because they walk in zeal for the Lord and abstain from what God hateth and forbiddeth by His commandments. The single face is the single eye that fills the whole body with light, and the clean creature is read straight off Torah's law of clean and unclean. It ain't new — the single-faced man Asher commends keeps the very commandments of God that mark clean from unclean.

threads.title: Asher's own walk — singleness of face, searching out the commandments
threads.summary_md: Asher closes his teaching on the two by witnessing to his own life: he proved all these things, wandered not from the truth of the Lord, and searched out the commandments of the Most High, walking with singleness of face unto good. The man who keeps one face is the doer who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues in it, blessed in his deed. It ain't new — Asher's singleness of face is a life spent searching out and keeping the commandments, the doer's path the apostle commends.

threads.title: Keep the law of the Lord — the double-faced sin twofold
threads.summary_md: Asher exhorts his children to keep the commandments and the law of the Lord, following truth with singleness of face, for the double-faced are guilty of a twofold sin — both doing evil and delighting in those who do it. The apostle marks the same double guilt of those who not only do such things but have pleasure in them that do them, and James calls the wavering, double-minded man unstable. It ain't new — Asher's charge to keep the law with one face is the apostolic call away from the twofold sin of the divided heart.

threads.title: The latter end of a man — the angel of peace and eternal life
threads.summary_md: Asher tells how the latter ends of men show their righteousness: the troubled soul departs to torment by the evil spirit it served, but the peaceful soul meets the angel of peace, who leads it into eternal life. The two ways run all the way to the two ends Moses set before Israel — life and death — and to the eternal life laid up for them that love the Lord. It ain't new — the two destinies Asher sees at death are the life and death Deuteronomy set before every soul, and the crown of life the apostle promises.

threads.title: Scattered to the four corners — set at nought as useless water
threads.summary_md: Asher's closing prophecy is the two-house word: Israel shall sin, be delivered to its enemies, its land made desolate and holy places destroyed, and be scattered to the four corners of the earth, set at nought in the dispersion as useless water — scattered like Gad and Dan, no longer knowing land, tribe, or tongue. This is precisely the curse Moses spoke for forsaking the law. It ain't new — the scattering Asher foresees is the dispersion Deuteronomy and Leviticus pronounced for despising the commandments.

threads.title: The Lord shall gather you in faith through His tender mercy
threads.summary_md: After the scattering, Asher's hope: the Lord will gather you together in faith through His tender mercy, for the sake of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This is the second word of the two-house promise — Moses foretold not only the scattering but the return and gathering when Israel turns, and the prophets see the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah gathered from the four corners and made one nation again. It ain't new — the gathering Asher promises is the return Deuteronomy and the prophets bound up in God's mercy to the fathers.

threads.title: The Most High shall visit, break the head of the dragon, and save Israel and the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: At the centre of Asher's hope the Most High Himself shall visit the earth, break the head of the dragon in the water, and save Israel and all the Gentiles. Some later hands gloss this as God walking as man; the genuine root is the prophets' word that the Lord shall slay the dragon in the sea, and that His salvation reaches both Israel and the nations through the root of Jesse. It ain't new — the Most High visiting to crush the serpent and save both Israel and the Gentiles is the prophets' own hope, fulfilled in the Anointed One.

threads.title: Joseph's confession — hated by his brethren, but the Lord was with him
threads.summary_md: Joseph opens his deathbed testament with the litany of his life: his brethren hated him and would have slain him, they let him into a pit and sold him into slavery, yet at every turn Yahuah delivered, nourished, comforted, and exalted him. It ain't new — this is the very arc Moses set down in Genesis and the Psalmist sang of the man sold for a servant whom the word of Yahuah tried.

threads.title: He struggled against a shameless woman, and God delivered him
threads.summary_md: Pharaoh's captain entrusts his house to Joseph, and at once Joseph struggles against the shameless woman who urges him to transgress — the temptation Genesis records, here owned as a fire from which the God of Israel delivered him. Cast into prison, beaten, mocked, he still finds mercy with the keeper. It ain't new — Moses already told both the refusal and the favour Joseph found in the prison.

threads.title: Threatened day by day, he remembered his father's words and prayed
threads.summary_md: The Egyptian woman threatens, flatters, and offers him lordship of her house, but Joseph remembers his father's words, weeps and prays, fasts, drinks no wine, and gives his food to the poor and sick. Genesis says she spake to Joseph day by day, and he hearkened not — the testament fills in the disciplines by which he held fast. It ain't new — youthful lusts are fled by the pure heart that seeks Yahuah early.

threads.title: The Lord takes no pleasure in adultery, but in the pure heart
threads.summary_md: The woman flatters Joseph as a holy man, then offers to leave her idols and walk in the law of his Lord if only he will lie with her. Joseph answers that Yahuah wills no uncleanness, takes no pleasure in adultery, but delights in those who approach Him with a pure heart and undefiled lips. It ain't new — the commandment is a lamp that keeps a man from the flattering tongue of the strange woman.

threads.title: The wickedness of the ungodly has no power over those who worship with chastity
threads.summary_md: The woman sends food laced with enchantments, but the God of Joseph's fathers reveals her wickedness by His angel; Joseph eats it openly, calling on the God of his fathers and the angel of Abraham, to prove that no ungodly device prevails against those who worship God with chastity. It ain't new — God is faithful in temptation and makes the way of escape for them that fear Him in darkness and in bonds.

threads.title: He left his garment behind and fled away naked
threads.summary_md: She lays hold of his garments and forcibly drags him; Joseph leaves the garment behind and flees away naked, and on the strength of that garment she falsely accuses him, and he is scourged and sent to Pharaoh's prison. This is the very scene of Genesis 39 — the caught garment, the flight, the false charge, the prison. It ain't new — Moses already set down the garment left in her hand.

threads.title: God loves him who in a den of darkness combines fasting with chastity
threads.summary_md: Even from prison she keeps soliciting, offering freedom for consent, but not in thought does Joseph incline to her; God loves the man who in a den of darkness joins fasting with chastity more than the man who in kings' chambers joins luxury with licence, and Yahuah guards Joseph from all her devices. It ain't new — youthful lust is fled by following righteousness with a pure heart, and the tried man receives the crown of life.

threads.title: Sold, he refrained from telling he was the son of Jacob
threads.summary_md: Joseph turns from the chastity narrative to its fruit: how great things patience and prayer with fasting work, so that the Most High dwells with the chaste and exalts him. He marks his own restraint — though loved above his brethren and being sold by them, he did not raise himself against them with evil intent, but out of respect refused to tell the Ishmaelites that he was the son of Jacob. It ain't new — this is the Joseph who would say, ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good.

threads.title: He confessed himself a slave that he might not put his brethren to shame
threads.summary_md: Joseph exhorts his sons to fear God and honour their brethren, for every one who does the law of Yahuah is loved by Him. He recalls that when the Ishmaelites asked whether he was a slave, he answered that he was a home-born slave, that he might not put his brethren to shame — choosing his own dishonour over their exposure. It ain't new — to love thy neighbour as thyself, and to bear long with a brother's fault, is the whole of the law.

threads.title: His bowels melted, yet he restrained himself for his brethren's sake
threads.summary_md: The Ishmaelites tell Joseph that his father mourns him in sackcloth; his bowels are dissolved and his heart melts, and he longs to weep — yet he restrains himself, still saying "I am a slave," that he should not put his brethren to shame. This is the very tenderness Genesis records when Joseph at last could not refrain himself. It ain't new — the Messiah-type silently bears his own grief rather than expose those who wronged him.

threads.title: He returned their money, upbraided them not, and comforted them
threads.summary_md: Joseph charges his sons to love one another and with long-suffering hide one another's faults, for God delights in the unity of brethren. When his brethren came into Egypt he returned their money, upbraided them not, and comforted them; after Jacob's death he loved them yet more, counting their children his, their suffering his, and exalting not himself but being among them as one of the least. It ain't new — this is Joseph who comforted them and spake kindly, the Messiah-type who forgives and saves.

threads.title: If any seek to do you evil, do well unto him and pray for him
threads.summary_md: Joseph's closing charge: walk in the commandments of Yahuah, and if any one seeks to do you evil, do well unto him and pray for him, and you shall be redeemed of Yahuah from all evil. He points to himself — out of humility and long-suffering God gave him a wife, gold, beauty, and length of days. It ain't new — to love your enemies and overcome evil with good is the Messiah's own word, the fruit of Joseph's whole long-suffering life.

threads.title: The vision — from a virgin a lamb is born, and a lion at his hand
threads.summary_md: Joseph's deathbed vision: from Judah a virgin in a linen garment, and from her a spotless lamb; at his left hand as it were a lion; all the beasts rush against him, and the lamb overcomes and treads them under foot. The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world and the Lion of the tribe of Judah are seen together centuries before the cross. It ain't new — Moses, Isaiah, and the prophets had already drawn the virgin, the lamb, and the lion of Judah.

threads.title: Ye shall carry up my bones with you out of Egypt
threads.summary_md: Joseph dies at a good old age with a charge: God will visit Israel and bring them into the land He promised the fathers, and they shall carry up his bones with them. So it came to pass — at the Exodus the children of Israel took the bones of Joseph and buried him among his fathers. It ain't new — Moses kept this oath and carried up the bones, and Joshua laid them in the ground of the inheritance.

threads.title: Rachel's barren years, her prayer, and the son of her sorrow
threads.summary_md: Benjamin opens by retelling Moses exactly: Rachel barren after Joseph, her long-withheld womb opened in answer to prayer, and her death in giving him birth on the way to Ephrath. Genesis even keeps the two names — Ben-oni, the son of her sorrow, and Benjamin, the name his father gave. It ain't new — the testament only confesses on the deathbed the very birth the Torah had already written.

threads.title: The bloodied coat and the brother sold to the Ishmaelites
threads.summary_md: Joseph tells Benjamin what the brothers reported to Jacob — that they dipped the coat in blood — and what they truly did: stripped him of it and gave him to the Ishmaelites. The testament simply gives Joseph's voice to the deeds Moses records. It ain't new — the dabbled coat and the selling are the Torah's own account of the wrong Joseph would later forgive.

threads.title: Love the Lord God and keep His commandments, love thy neighbour
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's whole charge stands on the two great commands: love the Lord God of heaven and earth and keep His commandments, and love thy neighbour. The man who does both — the example is Joseph — cannot be ruled by the spirit of Beliar, for he is shielded by the fear of God. It ain't new — this is Moses and the Prophets in two clauses, the very pair the Messiah named the whole law and the prophets hang upon.

threads.title: Joseph besought his father to pray that their sin be not imputed
threads.summary_md: The mark of the good man, says Benjamin, is that Joseph asked Jacob to pray that the Lord would not impute to his brethren the evil they did him — the man who was sold interceding for those who sold him. Genesis sets the pattern: Joseph weeps, comforts, and forgives, naming the very providence that turned their evil to good. It ain't new — the mercy that returns good for evil and prays for the offender is the Torah's love-of-neighbour carried to its height.

threads.title: A blameless one delivered up for lawless men, for the salvation of all
threads.summary_md: Jacob's blessing over Joseph reaches past Joseph: a prophecy that a blameless one shall be delivered up for lawless men, a sinless one die for the ungodly, for the salvation of the Gentiles and of Yashar'el (Israel), to destroy Beliar. Joseph is the good man who was sold and forgave, and the prophecy points beyond him to the Branch from Levi and Yahudah (Judah), the Anointed delivered up and raised. It ain't new — *He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth* (Isaiah 53:7) — the lamb led to the slaughter in Isaiah is the one Joseph's life points to.

threads.title: The good man hath not a dark eye, for he showeth mercy to all
threads.summary_md: The good man, Benjamin says, hath not a dark eye but shows mercy to all men, even sinners; on the poor he has mercy, on the weak compassion. The Messiah's own teaching turns on the same image — the single eye that fills the whole body with light — and on the mercy that obtains mercy. It ain't new — the bright eye and the merciful heart are the Torah's love of neighbour seen plainly.

threads.title: By doing good he overcometh evil, and envieth not
threads.summary_md: Though men devise evil against him, the good man overcomes evil by doing good, and he envies none — not the glorified, not the rich, not the valiant. Paul writes the same charge to the Romans almost word for word: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good. It ain't new — the apostle's rule of the renewed mind is the deathbed wisdom of Benjamin.

threads.title: The holy man is merciful to his reviler; humbled a little, glorified after
threads.summary_md: The good mind disarms even the violent: the holy man is merciful to his reviler and holds his peace, and the betrayed righteous man prays — humbled for a little, but soon appearing far more glorious, as Joseph was. Joseph in the pit and prison, then over Egypt, is the very pattern; and the Messiah, reviled and silent, then ascending in glory, is its fulfilment. It ain't new — the abasement-before-exaltation of the righteous runs from Joseph through the Servant of Isaiah.

threads.title: One disposition, uncorrupt and pure — no double tongue, no double sight
threads.summary_md: The good mind, Benjamin teaches, has not two tongues of blessing and cursing, nor double sight nor double hearing; it has one disposition, pure toward all men, for the Lord is its portion. James names the same single-heartedness against the double-minded man, and the Messiah against the tongue that says more than yea and nay. It ain't new — the undivided heart whose portion is the Lord is the longing of the Psalms.

threads.title: Cain delivered to sevenfold vengeance — the wages of brother-hatred
threads.summary_md: Benjamin warns that the sword of Beliar is the mother of seven evils, and grounds the warning in Cain, delivered to sevenfold vengeance and Lamech to seventy times seven — and all who are like Cain in envy and hatred of brethren fall under the same judgment. Genesis sets the sevenfold and seventy-sevenfold; John names plainly what brother-hatred is. It ain't new — that the hater of his brother is a murderer is written from the first blood spilled in the field.

threads.title: The pure mind looketh not after a woman to fornication
threads.summary_md: He that has a pure mind in love, Benjamin says, looks not after a woman with a view to fornication, for the Spirit of God rests on him; as the sun is undefiled though it shine on mire, so the pure mind cleanses and is not defiled. The Messiah set the same standard at the root, in the heart that looks. It ain't new — purity of heart, not merely of deed, is the law's own measure, and the pure in heart shall see God.

threads.title: From the words of Enoch the righteous — the fornication of Sodom
threads.summary_md: Benjamin names his source: the words of Enoch the righteous, foreseeing that his sons will commit the fornication of Sodom and renew wanton deeds with women. Enoch's own book records the fornication and the defiling with women that filled the earth with corruption, and Jude couples Sodom's strange flesh with the angels who left their estate. It ain't new — Benjamin reads the latter-day apostasy out of Enoch, the very witness the apostle Jude would later quote by name.

threads.title: The last temple more glorious, the twelve tribes and all Gentiles gathered
threads.summary_md: Yet the temple of God shall be in their portion, and the last temple more glorious than the first; there the twelve tribes shall be gathered, and all the Gentiles, until the Most High sends forth His salvation. Haggai promised the latter house greater than the former, and Isaiah saw all nations flowing to the mountain of the Lord's house. It ain't new — the two-house ingathering of all twelve tribes with the nations is the prophets' settled hope.

threads.title: The Lord lifted up upon a tree, and the veil of the temple rent
threads.summary_md: The prophecy then darkens: the Lord shall be treated with outrage and lifted up upon a tree, and the veil of the temple rent, and the Spirit pass to the Gentiles as fire poured forth. The Anointed of Levi and Judah is the one lifted up; Moses already wrote that the hanged one bears a curse, and the Gospel records the veil torn from top to bottom at the very hour. It ain't new — the tree, the curse borne, and the rent veil are written in the Torah and fulfilled in the Branch.

threads.title: The Spirit to the Gentiles, and He shall ascend from Hades into heaven
threads.summary_md: The Spirit of God shall pass to the Gentiles as fire poured forth, and He shall ascend from Hades and pass from earth into heaven — lowly upon earth, glorious in heaven. Paul reads the same descent and ascent into the lower parts and up far above the heavens, and Peter tells how He preached to the spirits in prison. It ain't new — the One who descends and ascends, pouring the Spirit on the nations, is the hope the prophets and apostles share.

threads.title: Keep the law and commandments, the fathers' inheritance, till salvation comes
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's dying charge is the fathers' charge: keep the law of the Lord and His commandments, the inheritance Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob handed down — until the Lord reveal His salvation to all Gentiles. Moses set the same commandment as Israel's very life, and Isaiah promised the Servant given for a light to the Gentiles. It ain't new — the keeping of the commandments and the salvation reaching the nations are one inheritance from the fathers.

threads.title: Enoch, Noah, and the fathers rise — each one over his tribe
threads.summary_md: Then, Benjamin says, you shall see Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rising on the right hand in gladness, and we also rise, each one over his tribe, worshipping the King of heaven. The Messiah declared God the God of the living, not the dead — the fathers live to Him — and promised the twelve to sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes. It ain't new — the rising of the fathers and the twelve set over the tribes is the resurrection hope the Gospel confirms.

threads.title: All men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame
threads.summary_md: The resurrection is universal: all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame, and the Lord shall judge Israel first for their unrighteousness. Daniel saw the sleepers awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame; the Messiah named the resurrection of life and the resurrection of damnation; John saw the dead, small and great, judged out of the books. It ain't new — the twofold rising to glory or shame is Daniel's own vision, sealed in the prophets and the apostles.

threads.title: He shall convict Israel through the chosen ones of the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: Then He shall judge the Gentiles, and convict Israel through the chosen ones of the Gentiles — those who believed entering into the portion of them that fear the Lord. Paul writes the same mystery: through Israel's fall salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy, that Israel might be saved. It ain't new — that the believing nations would stir Israel to her own salvation is the apostle's mystery, foreseen here on Benjamin's deathbed.

threads.title: All Israel gathered to the Lord, the ravening wolf no more
threads.summary_md: If they walk in holiness, Benjamin says, all Israel shall be gathered unto the Lord, and he shall no longer be called a ravening wolf but a worker distributing food. Jacob's blessing had named Benjamin a wolf that ravins; Moses promised the scattered would be gathered when they returned, and Ezekiel saw the tribes made one. It ain't new — the gathering of all Israel and the turning of the wolf to a feeder is the prophets' restoration applied to Benjamin's own line.

threads.title: One beloved of the Lord shall arise, enlightening the Gentiles
threads.summary_md: Benjamin foresees one beloved of the Lord arising in the latter days, a doer of His good pleasure, enlightening the Gentiles, going to and fro among the synagogues of the nations, inscribed in the holy books, a chosen one of God for ever. Moses had called Benjamin the beloved of the Lord; and from Benjamin's seed came the apostle Paul, of that very tribe, whose work and word stand written in the scriptures and carried the light to the Gentiles. It ain't new — the beloved of Benjamin dwelling in safety is Moses' blessing, ripening into the apostle of the nations.

threads.title: Carry up my bones out of Egypt and bury me with my fathers
threads.summary_md: Benjamin's last command is the patriarchs' command: carry up my bones out of Egypt and bury me at Hebron, near my fathers — and the sons brought up the bones of all their fathers during the Canaanitish war. Joseph had bound Israel by oath to carry up his bones, Moses kept it, and they were buried in the land at the last. It ain't new — the carrying-up of the fathers' bones to the land of promise is the oath that runs from Joseph to the conquest.

threads.title: The Inspired Reason — the mind disciplined under the Law
threads.summary_md: The book opens its thesis: *whether the Inspired Reason is supreme ruler over the passions* (4 Maccabees 1:1). But this Reason is no Stoic autonomy standing apart from the Creator; the writer names its source plainly — *This I take to be the culture acquired under the Law, through which we learn with due reverence the things of Elohim (God)* (4 Maccabees 1:4). The mind that masters lust and rage and fear is the mind trained BY the Torah. It ain't new: Paul says the same — *the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good* (Romans 7:12), and *I delight in the law of Elohim (God) after the inward man* (Romans 7:22), warring against *the law of sin which is in my members* (Romans 7:23). David sang it long before — *The law of Yahuah (LORD) is perfect, converting the soul* (Psalm 19:7) — and Solomon weighed self-mastery higher than conquest — *he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city* (Proverbs 16:32). Moses set the whole charge near, not far off — *the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it* (Deuteronomy 30:14). The Torah-trained reason is the oldest wisdom there is.

threads.title: Reason the master-gardener — ruling, not uprooting, the passions
threads.summary_md: 4 Maccabees is careful: Reason does *not* extirpate the passions but enables us to resist them — *its action in their case is not to extirpate the passions, but to enable us to resist them successfully* (4 Maccabees 1:2). The picture is the disciplined garden: *each man's Reason as master-gardener, weeding and pruning and binding up... brings the thicket of dispositions and passions under domestication* (4 Maccabees 1:7), *For while Reason is the guide of the virtues it is master of the passions* (4 Maccabees 1:7). It ain't new: Paul names the same walk — not the killing of all desire but the Spirit's mastery over the flesh — *Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh* (Galatians 5:16), *the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh* (Galatians 5:17), with its harvest of *love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith* (Galatians 5:22). And the man who rules himself is the proverb's true conqueror — *he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city* (Proverbs 16:32). The husbandry of the heart is an old craft.

threads.title: The forbidden meats abstained from under the Law
threads.summary_md: The thesis lands at once on the dinner table: the first proof that Reason masters the body is the refusal of unclean food — *when we are tempted towards forbidden meats, how do we come to relinquish the pleasures to be derived from them? Is it not that Reason has power to repress the appetites?* (4 Maccabees 1:8), *Accordingly when we feel a desire to eat water-animals and birds and beasts and meats of every description forbidden to us under the Law, we abstain through the predominance of Reason* (4 Maccabees 1:9). The abstaining is *under the Law* — not a private scruple but the Creator's command, the same line Eleazar and the seven brothers will die for. It ain't new: the swine is named unclean from Sinai — *And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you* (Leviticus 11:7), *Of their flesh shall ye not eat, and their carcase shall ye not touch; they are unclean to you* (Leviticus 11:8); Moses repeats it — *Thou shalt not eat any abominable thing* (Deuteronomy 14:3). And Daniel, in a tyrant's court, set the pattern of the disciplined refusal — *Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat* (Daniel 1:8). The martyrs' table-faith is the oldest obedience there is — it ain't new.

threads.title: Joseph's Reason and the Tenth Word — Thou shalt not covet
threads.summary_md: The first proof that Reason masters every passion is Joseph: *This, certainly, is why we praise the virtuous Joseph, because by his Reason, with a mental effort, he checked the carnal impulse* (4 Maccabees 2:1), *a young man at the age when physical desire is strong, by his Reason quenched the impulse of his passions* (4 Maccabees 2:1). And the writer grounds that mastery not in Stoic willpower but in the Torah itself, quoting the Decalogue: *For the Law says, 'Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor anything that is thy neighbour's'* (4 Maccabees 2:1). It ain't new: Joseph fled the very temptation centuries before the philosophers wrote — *his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me* (Genesis 39:7), and he answered, *how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against Elohim (God)?* (Genesis 39:9), and *he left his garment in her hand, and fled* (Genesis 39:12). And the word the writer cites is the Tenth Word spoken at Sinai — *Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife* (Exodus 20:17), repeated by Moses — *Neither shalt thou desire thy neighbour's wife* (Deuteronomy 5:21). The Torah is what trains the reason to flee — it ain't new.

threads.title: The Law overrules greed — debt-release and gleaning for the poor
threads.summary_md: The Law does not merely restrain lust; it reaches into the purse. The writer argues that the Torah teaches even the miser and the grasping man to act against their nature: *as soon as a man orders his life according to the Law, if he is miserly he acts contrary to his nature, and lends money to the needy without interest, and at the seventh-year periods cancels the debt* (4 Maccabees 2:2), and *if he is parsimonious, he is overruled by the Law... and refrains from gleaning his stubbles or picking the last grapes from his vineyards* (4 Maccabees 2:2). It ain't new: the seventh-year release is Moses' own statute — *At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release* (Deuteronomy 15:1), *Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it... because it is called the LORD'S release* (Deuteronomy 15:2). And the law of the corner and the gleanings is from Sinai — *thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest* (Leviticus 19:9), *thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape of thy vineyard; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger* (Leviticus 19:10), which Moses applies to the forgotten sheaf and the olive boughs — *it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow* (Deuteronomy 24:19). The Torah's mastery over greed is the oldest charity there is — it ain't new.

threads.title: The Law governs anger — Moses at Dathan and Abiram, Jacob over Simeon and Levi
threads.summary_md: Reason ruling through the Law masters even rage. The writer reaches for two examples from Moses' own books: *Moses when he was angered against Dathan and Abiram did not give free course to his wrath, but governed his anger by his Reason* (4 Maccabees 2:4), and *our wise father Jacob blame[d] the houses of Simeon and Levi for their unreasoning slaughter of the tribe of the Shechemites, saying, 'Accursed be their anger!'* (4 Maccabees 2:4). It ain't new: when Dathan and Abiram rose against him, Moses ruled his spirit — *And they rose up before Moses... two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly* (Numbers 16:2); the defiant *We will not come up* (Numbers 16:12) did not provoke unbridled wrath but a governed appeal to Yahuah. And Jacob's curse on his sons' fury is in his blessing — *Simeon and Levi are brethren; instruments of cruelty are in their habitations* (Genesis 49:5), *Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel* (Genesis 49:7) — for *Simeon and Levi... slew all the males* of Shechem (Genesis 34:25). The Torah-trained reason that restrains rage is the patriarchs' own discipline — it ain't new.

threads.title: Elohim implanted the passions and gave the Law at creation
threads.summary_md: The chapter closes at the root of the whole argument: the Creator who made the passions also gave the Law to govern them. *For in the day when Elohim (God) created man, he implanted in him his passions and inclinations* (4 Maccabees 2:5), *and also, at the very same time, set the mind on a throne amidst the senses to be his sacred guide in all things; and to the mind he gave the Law, by the which if a man order himself, he shall reign over a kingdom that is temperate, and just, and virtuous, and brave* (4 Maccabees 2:5). The passions are not evil to be killed but a trust to be ruled — by the Law given with them at creation. It ain't new: man is the Creator's own forming — *And Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul* (Genesis 2:7) — and set in the garden under command — *And Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed* (Genesis 2:8). The same Lawgiver who made the heart set life and death before it — *I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life* (Deuteronomy 30:19). The Law is the Creator's gift to the creature he formed — it ain't new.

threads.title: David's thirst, and the water poured out as an offering
threads.summary_md: To show that Reason controls but does not extirpate desire, the writer sets forth *the case of the thirst of King David.* Burning with *an intense thirst,* David craved the water held by the enemy, and two mighty warriors *scaled the enemy's ramparts* and *drew from it a draught for the king.* But David, judging the draught *reckoned as equivalent to blood* to be *a grievous danger to his soul,* and *opposing his Reason to his desire, he poured out the water as an offering to Elohim.* The Torah-trained mind masters the appetite without destroying it. It ain't new — Samuel and the Chronicler record the very deed: the three mighty men broke through the host, and David *would not drink thereof, but poured it out unto Yahuah,* saying *is not this the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives?*

threads.title: Reason rules the appetite — the antagonist of the passions
threads.summary_md: The writer grants that *none of you is able to extirpate our natural desire,* nor anger, nor a malevolent disposition — but *Reason is not the extirpator of the passions, but their antagonist,* able to *quench the fires of desire, and to wrestle victoriously with the pangs of our bodies.* This is the Torah-trained mind ruling the appetite, not Stoic autonomy. It ain't new — Solomon weighed *he that ruleth his spirit* above *he that taketh a city,* and David sang that *the law of Yahuah is perfect, converting the soul.*

threads.title: Apollonius at the treasury — angels guard the Holy Place
threads.summary_md: A traitorous Simon informs the governor Apollonius that the Jerusalem treasury holds *many thousands of private deposits, not belonging to the temple account, and rightfully the property of King Seleucus* (4 Maccabees 4:2); Apollonius marches in to seize the moneys, but *there appeared from heaven angels, riding upon horses, with lightning flashing from their arms, and cast great fear and trembling upon them* (4 Maccabees 4:4), and he falls down half-dead and entreats the Hebrews to intercede for him. This is the very episode the sibling book tells: Simon's quarrel with the high priest, the boast of the treasury, the king's man sent to take the money, the priests' prayer, and the dread horseman from heaven who strikes him down. The deliverer-by-intercession even survives because the high priest pleads for him. It ain't new — the same hand that *defendeth* the place and *beateth and destroys them that come to hurt it* (2 Maccabees 3:39) turned back the spoiler in both tellings.

threads.title: Antiochus Epiphanes — the vile king who profanes the sanctuary
threads.summary_md: Seleucus dies and his successor is *his son Antiochus Epiphanes, an overweening terrible man* (4 Maccabees 4:9), who sells the high-priesthood, lays a gymnasium on the holy Mount, *abolished the service of the temple* (4 Maccabees 4:13), and *made a decree denouncing the penalty of death upon any who should be seen to live after the Law of our fathers* (4 Maccabees 4:16). Daniel had already drawn this king to the life: a *vile person* who comes in *by flatteries*, sets his heart *against the holy covenant*, pollutes the sanctuary, takes away the daily sacrifice, and corrupts the lawless *by flatteries* — yet the people who know their Elohim stay strong. It ain't new — the persecutor of 4 Maccabees is the very horn Daniel saw rise to *speak marvellous things against the Elohim of gods* (Daniel 11:36) before he comes to his end.

threads.title: The persecution begins — circumcision, the Law, and unclean meats
threads.summary_md: Antiochus plunders the city and turns to break the people: women *for circumcising their sons... were flung, together with their offspring, headlong from the rocks* (4 Maccabees 4:17), and he *personally tried to force by tortures each man separately to eat unclean meats and thus abjure the Yahudi (Jewish) religion* (4 Maccabees 4:18). Both sibling books tell the same assault: he comes up against Jerusalem with a great multitude after striking Egypt, plunders the sanctuary, decrees that all leave the Law, slays the women who circumcised their children, and would compel them to *eat swine's flesh, and unclean beasts*. The martyrs who fill the rest of 4 Maccabees die rather than defile themselves with forbidden food — the Creator's dietary law standing firm. It ain't new — the very crisis was already chronicled, and Israel *chose rather to die, that they might not be defiled with meats* (1 Maccabees 1:63).

threads.title: ★ The Divine Law accepted as the Law of our country
threads.summary_md: Dragged before Antiochus and urged to the *unlawful eating of unclean meat,* the aged priest Eleazar answers for his people: *We, O Antiochus, having accepted the Divine Law as the Law of our country, do not believe any stronger necessity is laid upon us than that of our obedience to the Law.* He counts no transgression small: *the transgression of the Law, be it in small things or in great, is equally heinous; for in either case equally the Law is despised.* This is the very opposite of the law-against-grace reading — the martyr will die rather than despise one statute. It ain't new — *the law of Yahuah is perfect, converting the soul,* and Moses set it before the people as *thy life, and the length of thy days,* the word *very nigh unto thee... that thou mayest do it.*

threads.title: The Law teaches self-control, justice, and to worship the only Elohim
threads.summary_md: To the tyrant's scoff that the Yahudi philosophy is contrary to reason, Eleazar replies: *Not so, for the Law teaches us self-control, so that we are masters of all our pleasures and desires... and it teaches justice, so that with all our various dispositions we act fairly, and it teaches righteousness, so that with due reverence we worship only the Elohim (God) who is.* The Torah-trained mind is not Stoic autonomy but discipline grounded in the Law — self-control, justice, righteousness, and the worship of the one Elohim. It ain't new — Moses taught *what doth Yahuah thy Elohim require of thee, but to fear* him *and to love him,* the Decalogue opens *Thou shalt have no other gods before me,* and Paul testifies *the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.*

threads.title: ★★ The Creator-Lawgiver gave the dietary law — clean and unclean stands
threads.summary_md: Eleazar grounds the refusal of swine's flesh not in custom but in creation: *Therefore do we eat no unclean meat; for believing our Law to be given by Elohim (God), we know also that the Creator of the world, as a Lawgiver, feels for us according to our nature. He has commanded us to eat the things that will be convenient for our souls, and he has forbidden us to eat meats that would be the contrary.* The clean/unclean distinction is the Maker's own statute, given for the good of his people — the martyr dies FOR it, never against it. It ain't new — *the swine... is unclean to you... of their flesh shall ye not eat,* Moses repeats *thou shalt not eat any abominable thing,* and Daniel before him *purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself.* Eleazar of 2 Maccabees, the same man, *spit it forth* rather than taste the unlawful.

threads.title: Swine's flesh and things offered to idols — no other gods
threads.summary_md: Antiochus' decree is double: *compel them to eat swine's flesh and things offered to idols,* and any who *refuse to defile themselves with the unclean things* were to be tortured and put to death. Eleazar's refusal guards both the dietary law and the first command — for the worship of *only the Elohim (God) who is* allows no eating at the idol's table. It ain't new — the Law's first words are *Thou shalt have no other gods before me* and *Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image,* and Paul will warn the saints they *cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils.*

threads.title: Sons of Abraham — die nobly for righteousness' sake
threads.summary_md: When the courtiers urge Eleazar to feign eating the swine's flesh and so save himself, the old man cries out: *May we sons of Abraham never have so evil a thought as with faint heart to counterfeit a part unseemly to us.* He will not *change and become in our own persons a pattern to the young of impiety,* nor *fail to defend the Divine Law unto the death,* but charges, *O sons of Abraham, do ye die nobly for righteousness' sake.* The identity is covenant-deep: the children of the promise made to Abraham, who are *of faith.* It ain't new — Yahuah swore *an everlasting covenant* to Abraham's seed, and *they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham.*

threads.title: Unclean meat refused — the Creator-Lawgiver's command
threads.summary_md: The courtiers offer a way out: *do thou feign only to partake of the swine's flesh, and so save thyself.* Eleazar refuses to *encourage them to eat unclean meat,* dying rather than touch what the Law forbids. The swine is named unclean by the Creator's own statute, and the martyr counts the dietary law no light thing but the Divine Law to be defended *unto the death.* It ain't new — *the swine... is unclean to you... of their flesh shall ye not eat,* and Daniel before him *purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself.*

threads.title: ★ Make my blood their purification — the ransom that is a type
threads.summary_md: With the fire reaching his bones, Eleazar lifts his eyes and prays: *Thou, O Elohim, knowest that though I might save myself I am dying by fiery torments for thy Law. Be merciful unto thy people, and let our punishment be a satisfaction in their behalf. Make my blood their purification, and take my soul to ransom their souls.* The righteous sufferer pleads his blood for the nation — yet this is only a shadow of the blood that truly purifies. The martyr's death points beyond itself to the Suffering Servant whose soul was made *an offering for sin,* and to the Messiah (Christ) in whom alone that foreshadowing is fulfilled. It ain't new — *he was wounded for our transgressions... he bare the sin of many,* and *to make reconciliation for iniquity* was foreseen long before; the martyr's plea borrows the pattern that the Messiah's own blood would at last complete.

threads.title: The Inspired Reason, master over the passions
threads.summary_md: Eleazar *nobly yielded up his spirit under the torture, and for the sake of the Law held out by his Reason even against the torments unto death.* The writer concludes: *the Inspired Reason is master over the passions,* for *his Reason having conquered his passions, we properly attribute to it the power of commanding them.* This Reason is no Stoic autonomy but the mind disciplined by the Torah, holding fast *for the sake of the Law.* It ain't new — *the law of Yahuah is perfect, converting the soul,* and *he that ruleth his spirit* is greater *than he that taketh a city.*

threads.title: He defiled not his holy teeth — the dietary law stands
threads.summary_md: In the praise of Eleazar the writer cries, *O priest worthy of thy priesthood, thou didst not defile thy holy teeth, nor didst thou befoul with unclean meat thy belly that had room only for piety and purity.* The aged confessor died rather than taste swine's flesh — not for a custom but because *Lev 11 / Deut 14 are the Creator-Lawgiver's command.* It ain't new — Moses wrote that *the swine... is unclean to you,* that *of their flesh shall ye not eat,* and bound the people to *sanctify yourselves, and... be holy; for I am holy* — the very holiness Eleazar would not befoul; Daniel before him *would not defile himself,* and his fellow Eleazar in the sister-book *spit forth* the abomination rather than eat.

threads.title: Aaron with the censer ran against the fiery angel and overcame
threads.summary_md: To magnify Eleazar the writer reaches for his priestly ancestor: *as our father Aaron, armed with the censer, ran through the massed congregation against the fiery angel and overcame him, so the son of Aaron, Eleazar, being consumed by the melting heat of the fire, remained unshaken in his Reason.* The son of Aaron stands in the fire as Aaron once stood between the dead and the living. It ain't new — Moses records the very deed: *Take a censer... and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from Yahuah,* and Aaron *ran into the midst of the congregation... and stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed.*

threads.title: With Isaac-like Reason — the Akedah as the martyr's charter
threads.summary_md: The aged Eleazar, his sinews unstrung, *grew a young man again in the spirit of his Reason and with Isaac-like Reason turned the hydra-headed torture to impotence.* The martyr's pattern is Isaac, who lay bound upon the wood and did not shrink. It ain't new — Moses tells how Abraham *bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar upon the wood,* and *stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son,* until the angel stayed him; and the apostle reads it as resurrection-faith, that Abraham offered Isaac *accounting that Elohim was able to raise him up, even from the dead* — the very hope that strengthened Eleazar in the flame.

threads.title: They die not, but live unto Elohim — the resurrection of the righteous
threads.summary_md: Here is the book's beating heart. They who *with their whole heart make righteousness their first thought... alone are able to master the weakness of the flesh, believing that unto Elohim they die not, as our patriarchs, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, died not, but that they live unto Elohim.* This is no Greek immortality but the resurrection hope of Moses and the Prophets. It ain't new — the Messiah Himself answered the resurrection from this very ground: *I am the Elohim of Abraham, and the Elohim of Isaac, and the Elohim of Jacob? Elohim is not the Elohim of the dead, but of the living,* for *all live unto him*; the whole heart is Moses' own command, *thou shalt love Yahuah Elohayka with all thine heart*; and the patriarchs *died in faith, not having received the promises,* yet sought *a better country, that is, an heavenly.*

threads.title: The seven brothers brought to eat unclean meat — the ancestral Law refused
threads.summary_md: The tyrant turns from Eleazar to the young — *he ordered the guards to bring others of the young men of the Hebrews, and if they would eat unclean meat to release them after eating it* (4 Maccabees 8:1-2). *Seven brethren together with their aged mother were brought prisoners before him* (4 Maccabees 8:1), and Antiochus, after his flattery fails, names the one demand that buys their lives — *positions of importance and authority in my service if you will reject the ancestral law of your polity* (4 Maccabees 8:2). The whole contest hangs on one point: eat the swine and live, or keep the Creator-Lawgiver's command and die. It ain't new: the swine is named unclean from Sinai — *And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you* (Leviticus 11:7), *Of their flesh shall ye not eat, and their carcase shall ye not touch; they are unclean to you* (Leviticus 11:8); Moses repeats it — *the swine... it is unclean unto you: ye shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their dead carcase* (Deuteronomy 14:8). Daniel set the pattern in another tyrant's court — *Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat* (Daniel 1:8). And this is the very scene 2 Maccabees records — *seven brothers with their mother were taken, and compelled by the king against the law to taste swine’s flesh* (2 Maccabees 7:1). The table-faith the brothers will die for is the oldest obedience there is — it ain't new.

threads.title: Choosing death over transgression — fear not them that kill the body
threads.summary_md: Antiochus arrays the engines of torture and adds a tempter's gloss — *the Justice you worship will pardon your unwilling transgression* (4 Maccabees 8:4) — and the writer rehearses the speech a coward might have made: *if compelled by necessity we yield to the king in fear... Even the Law itself does not willingly condemn us to death* (4 Maccabees 8:10–11,24). But that is not the brothers' mind — *no such words escaped these young men at the prospect of the torture... For they were despisers of the passions and masters over pain* (4 Maccabees 8:15–16). They will die before they transgress. It ain't new: the choice is the one Moses set before Yashar'el — *I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life* (Deuteronomy 30:19); the psalmist held the Law through deadly peril — *My soul is continually in my hand: yet do I not forget thy law* (Psalm 119:109), *The wicked have laid a snare for me: yet I erred not from thy precepts* (Psalm 119:110). And the Messiah named the fear that frees a martyr — *fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body* (Matthew 10:28). To prize the commandment above life itself is no new courage — it ain't new.

threads.title: Ready to die rather than transgress — the Law is life
threads.summary_md: The seven brothers answer the tyrant with one voice: *We are ready to die rather than transgress the commandments of our fathers* (4 Maccabees 9:1), for they will not shame their ancestors by failing to *walk in obedience to the Law and take Moses as our counsellor* (4 Maccabees 9:2); they count it *a thing harder to bear than death itself* to be given their life *in return for a breach of the Law* (4 Maccabees 9:4). This is no Stoic boast of mere endurance — it is Moses' own choice set before the people: life bound up with keeping the commandments, death with forsaking them. The dietary refusal that costs them their lives is the Creator-Lawgiver's command in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and the heart that would rather die than err from the precepts is the very heart of the psalmist. It ain't new — *therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live* (Deuteronomy 30:19) was the charter of these martyrs long before they were born.

threads.title: The first brother — fear not them that kill the body
threads.summary_md: Racked on the wheel till his bones are out of joint, the eldest brother denounces the tyrant as an *enemy of the justice of heaven* and dies declaring the guards' tortures *not strong enough to lead captive my Reason* (4 Maccabees 9:14–17); he charges his brothers to *war a holy and honourable warfare on behalf of righteousness, through which may the just Providence... become merciful unto his people and take vengeance on the accursed tyrant* (4 Maccabees 9:16), and the second brother in turn warns that the tyrant cannot *escape... the penalties of the divine wrath* (4 Maccabees 9:18). This is the Master's own teaching: fear not the man who can only kill the body but cannot touch the soul; and it is the patriarch's and prophet's confidence that Elohim will judge his people, raise the righteous who sleep, and avenge the blood of his servants. It ain't new — *fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul* (Matthew 10:28) was the courage Moses and the prophets had already breathed into Israel.

threads.title: The noble bond of brotherhood — suffering for the upbringing of Elohim
threads.summary_md: The third son, urged to taste and save himself, answers that *the same father begat me and my brothers that are dead, and the same mother gave us birth, and in the same doctrines was I brought up,* and so *I do not forswear the noble bond of brotherhood.* He offers his body to the engines, for *my soul ye cannot reach,* and dying he tells the tyrant: *We... suffer thus for our upbringing and our virtue that are of Elohim; but thou for thy impiety and thy cruelty shalt endure torments without end.* The same seven brothers in the sibling book confess the same hope and the same sentence on the king. It ain't new — *the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, to everlasting life,* and *Yahuah shall judge his people, and repent himself for his servants.*

threads.title: Elohim is a hearer of the speechless — the tongue cut out
threads.summary_md: When the fourth son will not deny *my noble brotherhood,* Antiochus bids them cut out his tongue. The young man answers, *Even if thou dost remove my organ of speech, Elohim is a hearer also of the speechless,* and lays it out ready, *for thou shalt not thereby silence my Reason.* He gives his members *to be mutilated for the cause of Elohim,* and warns, *Elohim will speedily pursue after thee; for thou cuttest out the tongue that sang songs of praise unto him.* The same torment befell the eldest brother in the sibling book. It ain't new — the Messiah told his own that when they are *brought before governors and kings,* it is *not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you,* and the blood of his servants is *known among the heathen... by the revenging.*

threads.title: We worship the Creator and live according to his virtuous Law
threads.summary_md: The fifth son springs forward and puts the charge to the tyrant: *Doth it seem evil to thee that we worship the Creator of all and live according to his virtuous Law?* For this they are *worthy of honours not of tortures.* He names what the king is: *now thou art Elohim's enemy and makest war on those that worship Elohim.* The martyr's whole crime is fidelity to the Lawgiver's Law and the worship of the one Creator. It ain't new — the same brothers in the sibling book warn the king *abide a while, and behold his great power, how he will torment you,* and Moses sang that *Yahuah shall judge his people, and repent himself for his servants.*

threads.title: Torture for not eating unclean meat — the Reason unconquered
threads.summary_md: The sixth son, *a mere boy,* tells the tyrant he is *as old in mind* as his brethren: *so if thou chooseth to torture us for not eating unclean meat, torture.* In the midst of the fire he cries that the brothers *in the cause of righteousness... have not been conquered,* and that the king's *impotence to alter our Reason or force us to eat unclean meat* is itself *an overthrow for thee.* The dietary refusal is no scruple but the Creator-Lawgiver's standing command, kept *unto death.* It ain't new — *the swine... is unclean to you... of their flesh shall ye not eat,* and the Messiah taught his own to *fear not them which kill the body.*

threads.title: The divine justice delivers thee to an eternal fire
threads.summary_md: The youngest son, brought to the red-hot brazier, indicts the king who would *take thy blessings and thy kingship at the hands of Elohim, and... slay his servants and torture the followers of righteousness.* For this, *the divine justice delivers thee unto a more rapid and an eternal fire and torments which shall not leave hold on thee to all eternity.* While the martyrs *have fulfilled their righteousness towards Elohim in their noble deaths,* the tyrant shall *miserably cry 'Woe is me!'* The sentence on the king is the same the same brothers pronounce in the sibling book. It ain't new — *many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt,* and *Yahuah... will torment you and your seed.*

threads.title: The Elohim of my fathers — be merciful unto my nation
threads.summary_md: Standing *on the brink of death,* the youngest declares, *I am no renegade to the witness borne by my brethren,* and prays: *I call upon the Elohim of my fathers to be merciful unto my nation. And thee will he punish both in this present life and after that thou art dead.* Then he *cast himself into the red-hot brazier, and so gave up the ghost.* The same youngest brother in the sibling book offers his body for the laws of his fathers, *beseeching Yahuah that he would speedily be merciful to our nation.* It ain't new — the plea for the nation, the doom on the persecutor, the body given for the laws of the fathers; *fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.*

threads.title: Let us imitate the Three Children who despised the furnace
threads.summary_md: As the seven cheer one another on, they reach for a remembered deliverance: *Let us imitate the Three Children at the Assyrian court who despised this same ordeal of the furnace. Let us not turn cravens before the proof of righteousness.* The pattern is fixed already in the Tanakh — Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego who would not bow, who answered the king *we are not careful to answer thee in this matter,* and who walked unburnt in the flame because the El Elyon went down with them. It ain't new — *if it be so, our Elohim whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace... but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods;* the brothers do not invent their courage, they imitate it.

threads.title: Isaac yielded himself — fear not the killer, the fathers shall receive us
threads.summary_md: Each brother stiffens the next with the memory of the Akedah and the certainty beyond death: *Remember of what stock ye are, and at whose fatherly hand Isaac for righteousness' sake yielded himself to be a sacrifice.* So they swear, *let us not fear him who thinketh he kills,* for *eternal torment awaits those who transgress the ordinance of Elohim,* and they look past the fire: *Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob shall receive us, and all our forefathers shall praise us.* The Akedah, the fear that is wrongly placed, the patriarchs who live to receive their sons — every clause is already written. It ain't new — Abraham *bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar,* the Messiah would say *fear not them which kill the body,* and *many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.*

threads.title: Brotherly love made strong by discipline under the Law
threads.summary_md: The writer traces the seven's fierce loyalty to its root: nature knit them at the breast, *nourished from the same blood,* *nursed together in arms,* but the bond was forged stronger still *through our discipline under the Law of Elohim.* *For trained in the same Law, and disciplined in the same virtues, and brought up together in the upright life, they loved one another the more abundantly.* The Law does not chill love — it is the very school that makes brotherly love fervent. It ain't new — *how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity,* *be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love,* and *we know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.*

threads.title: ★ A soul like Abraham — the mother unmoved by mother-love
threads.summary_md: The writer turns from the seven sons to their mother, marvelling that *even a woman's soul despised a yet greater diversity of pains; for the mother of the seven youths endured the torments inflicted on each several one of her children.* Though *the yearnings of a mother's heart* make her *feeling for her offspring... the centre of her whole world,* she stood firm: *she, the mother of those young men, with a soul like Abraham, was not moved from her purpose by her affection for her children.* The pattern named is the Akedah — Abraham who *withheld not* his only son when Elohim tried him, accounting that the Lawgiver could raise him. It ain't new — *thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me,* and the writer of the Hebrews knew this very martyrdom: *others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection.*

threads.title: ★ Religion dearer than her children — love of Elohim above kin
threads.summary_md: The writer cries out at the mother's choice: *O Reason of the sons, lord over the passions! O religion, that wast dearer to the mother than her children!* Set between *religion and the present saving alive of her seven sons,* she *loved rather religion, which saveth unto eternal life according to Elohim.* This is no cold heart — *through the fear of Elohim she rejected the present safety of her children* — but the very order the Law commands: the love of Yahuah above brother, son, daughter, or the wife of one's bosom. It ain't new — Moses charged that not even *thy son, or thy daughter* may turn the heart from Yahuah, and the Master said the same: *he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.*

threads.title: ★ A true daughter of Abraham — and the Ark that weathered the Deluge
threads.summary_md: Seeing her seven children destroyed, *the noble mother willingly surrendered them through faith in Elohim,* and *as a true daughter of Abraham, called to mind his Elohim-fearing courage.* The writer hails her *O mother of the race, vindicator of our Law, defender of our religion,* and crowns the figure with Noah: *as the Ark of Noah, with the whole living world for her burden in the world-whelming Deluge, did withstand the mighty surges, so thou, the keeper of the Law... didst nobly weather the storms.* Her courage is Abraham's at the Akedah, her steadfastness Noah's ark riding the flood. It ain't new — Abraham, tried, *withheld not* his only son, and Noah, *being warned of Elohim of things not seen as yet... prepared an ark to the saving of his house.*

threads.title: ★★ Abraham made haste to sacrifice Isaac — the Akedah, the martyrs' charter
threads.summary_md: The mother, urging her sons to die rather than transgress, reaches for the oldest pattern of all: *for whom also our father Abraham made haste to sacrifice his son Isaac, the ancestor of our nation; and Isaac, seeing his father's hand lifting the knife against him, did not shrink.* Father and son together upon Moriah — the one who offered and the one who yielded — become the model for these seven sons and their mother. The Akedah is no mere story to her; it is the charter of a faith that does not flinch at the knife, *accounting that Elohim was able to raise him up.* It ain't new — *Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son,* and by that very work *was faith made perfect.*

threads.title: Not so fierce the lions, not so hot the furnace — Daniel and the Three Children
threads.summary_md: Twice the mother measures her own ordeal against the Tanakh's great deliverances: *not so fierce were the lions around Daniel, not so hot was the burning fiery furnace of Mishael, as burned in her the instinct of motherhood.* And again she names them as proof to her sons: *And Daniel, the just man, was cast to the lions, and Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael were flung into the furnace of fire, and they endured for Elohim's sake.* The just who would not bow nor break their devotion are her witnesses that Elohim guards those who endure for his sake. It ain't new — *my Elohim hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths,* and the three came forth of the fire on whom *the fire had no power.*

threads.title: ★★ Men dying for Elohim live unto Elohim — as live Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
threads.summary_md: The chapter closes on the book's beating hope. The mother charges her sons to endure because *ye owe it to Elohim to endure all pain for his sake,* and the seven die *knowing well that men dying for Elohim live unto Elohim, as live Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the patriarchs.* Death for the sake of Elohim is no end but a passage into the life of the living — the patriarchs are not in the grave but with Elohim. This is the precise logic the Messiah pressed against the Sadducees, and the awakening Daniel foresaw. It ain't new — *Elohim is not the Elohim of the dead, but of the living,* and *many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake... to everlasting life.*

threads.title: ★ Starlike sons set in heaven — the resurrection of the righteous
threads.summary_md: The mother who watched all seven die is herself crowned in glory: *Not so majestic stands the moon amid the stars in heaven as thou, having lit the path of thy seven starlike sons unto righteousness, standest in honour with Elohim, and thou art set in heaven with them.* The prize they obtained through endurance was no earthly survival but *the prize of victory in incorruption in everlasting life.* This is the resurrection of the just, the very hope the writer of Hebrews points back to. It ain't new — *they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament... as the stars for ever and ever,* and *this corruptible must put on incorruption.*

threads.title: Righteousness gave the crown to her athletes
threads.summary_md: The contest is named: *And righteousness won the victory, and gave the crown to her athletes. Who but wondered at the athletes of the true Law?* The martyrs ran the holy course and finished it, and the wreath laid up for them is no perishing garland but the crown of life. It ain't new — Paul *fought a good fight* and looked for *a crown of righteousness,* and the faithful *unto death* are promised *a crown of life.*

threads.title: They stand beside the throne of Elohim
threads.summary_md: The reward is no mere memory but a present standing in glory: *whereby they now do both stand beside the throne of Elohim and live the blessed age.* And the writer grounds it in Moses' own word over the sanctified: *All also who have sanctified themselves are under thy hands.* The martyrs are gathered to the heavenly court, among the ranks that minister before the Ancient of days. It ain't new — the great multitude *stood before the throne,* the souls of the slain *lived and reigned,* and *all his saints are in thy hand.*

threads.title: ★★ A ransom for the nation — the type the Messiah fulfils
threads.summary_md: The book reaches its climax: the martyrs *having as it were become a ransom for our nation's sin; and through the blood of these righteous men and the propitiation of their death, the divine Providence delivered Yashar'el that before was evil entreated.* Here the righteous-sufferer whose blood delivers the people stands forth — yet *as it were,* only a shadow of the blood that truly delivers. The martyrs' death points forward to the Suffering Servant whose soul was made *an offering for sin* and who *bare the sin of many,* the propitiation that the Messiah (Christ) alone supplies. The writer of Hebrews knew this very martyrdom and saw beyond it to *a better resurrection.* It ain't new — *he was wounded for our transgressions... and with his stripes we are healed,* and to *make reconciliation for iniquity* was foreseen of old; the martyrs' blood borrows the pattern the Messiah's own blood at last completes.

threads.title: I kept guard over the rib that was builded into Eve — and the Serpent could not corrupt
threads.summary_md: The mother testifies of her own purity before she tells of her sons: *I was a pure maiden, and I strayed not from my father's house, and I kept guard over the rib that was builded into Eve.* No seducer, no deceiver, *nor did the false, beguiling Serpent sully the purity of my maidenhood.* She reaches straight back to the garden — the rib taken from Adam and made into a woman, and the subtil Serpent who beguiled her — and stands as the un-beguiled daughter of Eve. It ain't new — *the rib, which Yahuah Elohim had taken from man, made he a woman,* and the *serpent beguiled me, and I did eat* is the deceit she alone resisted.

threads.title: He taught you the Law and the prophets — the roll-call of the righteous
threads.summary_md: The mother recalls how the father, *while he was yet with us, taught you the Law and the prophets,* and named the cloud of witnesses one after another: *Abel who was slain by Cain,* *Isaac who was offered as a burnt-offering,* *Joseph in the prison,* *Phineas, the zealous priest,* the song of *Ananias, Azarias, and Mishael in the fire,* and *Daniel in the den of lions.* This is the catalogue of the righteous who suffered and were upheld — the very pattern the seven sons would walk. It ain't new — Abel's blood, the Akedah, Joseph's chains, Phineas' zeal, the three children in the furnace, and Daniel among the lions are all written in Moses and the prophets, the charter the martyrs inherited.

threads.title: Isaiah, David, Solomon, Ezekiel, Moses — the words that promise fire shall not hurt and the dead shall live
threads.summary_md: The father did not stop at the patriarchs; he *called to your minds the saying of Isaiah, "Yea even though thou pass through the fire, the flame shall not hurt thee,"* sang *the words of David... "Many are the afflictions of the just,"* quoted *the proverb of Solomon, "He is a tree of life to all them that do his will,"* confirmed *the words of Ezekiel, "Shall these dry bones live?"* and remembered *the song that Moses taught... "I will slay and I will make alive. This is your life."* Each is a near-verbatim quotation of the prophets — fire that cannot burn, the afflicted-but-delivered just, the tree of life for the obedient, the resurrection of the dry bones, and the Author of life and death. It ain't new — every line the father spoke is already written in Isaiah, the Psalms, the Proverbs, Ezekiel, and the song of Moses.

threads.title: ★ The sons of Abraham gathered to their fathers — a better resurrection
threads.summary_md: The tyrant's judgement is sure — *the judgement of Elohim pursued, and shall pursue, the accursed wretch* — but the martyrs' end is glory: *the sons of Abraham, with their victorious mother, are gathered together unto the place of their ancestors, having received pure and immortal souls from Elohim, to whom be glory for ever and ever.* They are gathered to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, awaiting the resurrection of the just. This is the very hope the writer of Hebrews names — those *tortured, not accepting deliverance,* that they might obtain *a better resurrection.* It ain't new — the faithful are *carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom,* and *many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake... to everlasting life.*

threads.title: Cain and Abel born outside Paradise
threads.summary_md: The Life of Adam and Eve opens where Genesis leaves off — outside the garden, the man knowing his wife and the first sons coming forth: *And Adam knew his wife Eve and went upwards to the sun-rising* (Adam and Eve 1:1-2), and *Eve conceived and bare two sons; Adiaphotos, who is called Cain and Amilabes who is called Abel* (Adam and Eve 1:1).
